models_evaluated: AI-LLM (chatbot, model not named in abstract)

links.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid reading level and reading ease of original vs AI-LLM patient-language reports
links.effect: Mean FKRL fell from 12.7 to 7.2 (X-ray), 13.4 to 7.5 (CT), 13.5 to 7.5 (MRI); FRE rose from 39.5 to 76.8, 27.3 to 73.1, 26.8 to 73.4; all statistically significant.
links.quote: Statistically significant improvements in mean FKRL scores in the AI-LLM generated X-ray report (12.7 ± 1.0-7.2 ± 0.6), CT report (13.4 ± 1.0-7.5 ± 0.5) and MRI report (13.5 ± 0.9-7.5 ± 0.6) were observed.

links.outcome: Reading grade level of AI-simplified reports versus original radiology reports
links.effect: Reading level dropped from about 13 (college level) to about 7.5 across modalities; FRE rose to 73-77.
links.quote: Statistically significant improvements in mean FRE scores in the AI-LLM generated X-ray report (39.5 ± 7.5-76.8 ± 5.1), CT report (27.3 ± 5.9-73.1 ± 5.6) and MRI report (26.8 ± 6.4-73.4 ± 5.0) were observed.

links.outcome: Hallucination or inaccurate text rate in AI-LLM-generated patient-language reports
links.effect: Hallucination rates were 2% (X-ray), 5% (CT) and 5% (MRI) of AI-generated reports.
links.quote: The hallucination rates in the AI-LLM generated X-ray report, CT report and MRI report were 2%, 5% and 5%, respectively.

unlisted_practices: Using an LLM to translate radiology reports into layman's terms for patients

screen.reason: The study evaluates an LLM's capability to simplify knee radiology reports for patients and documents readability metrics and hallucination rates, but it does not compare or evaluate a specific deployment practice or safeguard.
